FINDING_ID: LB_R2_F001  
SEVERITY: 0.78  
FLAW_CLASS: 1  
ABSTRACTION_INDEX: 0.73  
DESCRIPTION: `LoadBalancer._redundancy_target()` uses `K = len(self.models)` as the redundancy ceiling for critical and moderate tasks, but admissibility excludes PM when `K > 1`. As a result, for a pool with one PM and `n` admissible workers, critical tasks target `K` copies even though at most `n` are legally assignable, and moderate tasks use `ceil(K/2)` against total pool size rather than admissible pool size. This makes the target structurally unattainable in normal multi-model configurations and silently downgrades redundancy whenever assignment falls short; `_check_feasibility()` does not treat missed redundancy as a violation, so the returned allocation can appear feasible while under-covering critical tasks relative to the stated policy. This is distinct from prior findings about PM counting in `_admissibility_mask`: the bug here is that redundancy policy itself is parameterised by total models instead of admissible candidates for the specific task.  
PROPOSED_FIX: Compute redundancy targets from the per-task admissible model count, e.g. `K_adm = int(self._admissibility_mask()[j].sum())` or an equivalent helper, then cap targets by `K_adm`. Also add an explicit redundancy-feasibility check/report so unmet policy targets are surfaced separately from F1/F2/F3.  
VERIFIED: TRUE

FINDING_ID: LB_R2_F002  
SEVERITY: 0.72  
FLAW_CLASS: 5  
ABSTRACTION_INDEX: 0.69  
DESCRIPTION: `LoadBalancer._solve_greedy()` sorts tasks only by `criticality` descending and ignores `token_demand`. Under capacity constraints this can cause large high-criticality tasks to be stranded after smaller tasks of equal criticality consume fragmented capacity across models. Because the solver does not backtrack and only force-assigns when `assigned == 0`, it can return allocations with systematically reduced redundancy for large critical tasks even when a feasible higher-coverage allocation exists under a different ordering. This is a heuristic incompleteness issue in the core load-balancing path, not just suboptimal cost.  
PROPOSED_FIX: Use a stronger ordering heuristic, such as sorting by `(criticality desc, token_demand desc, redundancy_target desc)` or by a scarcity score based on admissible capacity. Better: perform a feasibility-first phase for high-criticality tasks with limited admissible capacity, or replace the greedy solver with ILP/CP-SAT for nontrivial instances.  
VERIFIED: TRUE

FINDING_ID: LB_R2_F003  
SEVERITY: 0.67  
FLAW_CLASS: 6  
ABSTRACTION_INDEX: 0.61  
DESCRIPTION: `LoadBalancer.__init__` accepts `role_map` without validating that every referenced model exists and every model has an explicit role. Missing entries silently default to `Role.PAR` in `_admissibility_mask()` via `self.role_map.get(model.model_id, Role.PAR)`. That default can accidentally expand admissibility and dispatch work to models whose intended role was unset, stale, or misspelled. Extra keys in `role_map` are also ignored silently. In a safety-oriented orchestration layer, role assignment drift should fail closed, not open.  
PROPOSED_FIX: Validate on construction that `set(role_map.keys()) == {m.model_id for m in models}` unless an explicit fail-open mode is configured. Reject unknown model IDs and missing assignments with a hard error. If a default is desired, default to the most restrictive role, not `PAR`.  
VERIFIED: TRUE

FINDING_ID: LB_R2_F004  
SEVERITY: 0.64  
FLAW_CLASS: 5  
ABSTRACTION_INDEX: 0.66  
DESCRIPTION: The objective and balancing logic treat a zero-capacity model (`L <= 0`) as having load fraction `0.0` in `_objective()` and `_balanced()`, while `_solve_greedy()` treats such models as `inf` load fraction for sorting. This internal inconsistency means zero-capacity models are deprioritised during assignment but then appear perfectly balanced in cost/balance evaluation if unassigned. The variance term can therefore understate imbalance by including dead models as zero-loaded/zero-fraction participants.  
PROPOSED_FIX: Use a single policy for `L <= 0` across solve and evaluation. Preferred options: exclude zero-capacity models from balancing statistics and admissibility altogether, or treat their fraction as `1.0`/undefined and fail validation early.  
VERIFIED: TRUE

FINDING_ID: LB_R2_F005  
SEVERITY: 0.61  
FLAW_CLASS: 2  
ABSTRACTION_INDEX: 0.58  
DESCRIPTION: `dispatch_check()` and `feasibility_probability()` are per-model/per-task-load utilities, but the allocation solver never uses them. Area 2 therefore has two contradictory notions of feasibility: deterministic hard-capacity checks in `_solve_greedy()`/`_check_feasibility()` and probabilistic pre-dispatch checks exposed separately. A caller can obtain an allocation that is “feasible” under hard `L` limits yet should be blocked under the configured uncertainty threshold, or vice versa. This split weakens the claimed “pre-dispatch probabilistic feasibility” extension because it is not integrated into the balancing decision itself.  
PROPOSED_FIX: Thread probabilistic feasibility into candidate admissibility or effective capacity during solve, e.g. exclude `(task, model)` assignments with `p < threshold`, or reduce usable capacity by a quantile bound derived from `L_std`. Ensure `solve()` and downstream dispatch checks use the same feasibility semantics.  
VERIFIED: TRUE

FINDING_ID: LB_R2_F006  
SEVERITY: 0.56  
FLAW_CLASS: 6  
ABSTRACTION_INDEX: 0.55  
DESCRIPTION: `validate_homogeneous()` is not a sound reduction test for the documented property “equal distribution optimal.” It checks only `balanced`, not that tasks are actually distributed equally or optimally. A degenerate allocation can pass if variance stays under `epsilon_bal`, especially with loose thresholds or small `k`. This weak validator can mask regressions in the solver while claiming the reduction property holds.  
PROPOSED_FIX: Strengthen the validator to assert expected per-model loads explicitly, verify no avoidable overload, and compare achieved objective against the analytically symmetric optimum for the constructed homogeneous instance.  
VERIFIED: TRUE

FINDING_ID: LB_R2_F007  
SEVERITY: 0.47  
FLAW_CLASS: 1  
ABSTRACTION_INDEX: 0.49  
DESCRIPTION: [UNVERIFIED cross-component] `LoadBalancer` stores `self.role_map = role_map` by reference rather than copying it. If the orchestrator mutates the shared role map between allocation steps or during asynchronous dispatch/recovery handling, admissibility and solve behavior may observe non-snapshot state. In this area alone I cannot prove concurrent use, but given prior mention of dynamic reassignment this is a realistic integration hazard.  
PROPOSED_FIX: Snapshot mutable inputs on construction, e.g. `self.role_map = dict(role_map)`, and pass versioned role assignments across components. If live mutation is intended, expose it explicitly with locking/version checks.  
VERIFIED: FALSE

FINDING_ID: LB_R2_F008  
SEVERITY: 0.44  
FLAW_CLASS: 6  
ABSTRACTION_INDEX: 0.46  
DESCRIPTION: The docstring for `_check_feasibility()` says it checks “all HARD feasibility constraints,” but redundancy targets are part of the allocator’s stated policy and are not checked at all. In practice the solver may under-achieve redundancy for critical tasks without any violation being reported, leaving callers unable to distinguish “fully policy-satisfied” from merely “covered at least once.” This is at minimum a specification/API mismatch and likely a policy enforcement gap.  
PROPOSED_FIX: Either (a) explicitly document redundancy as a soft objective, or (b) add an F4-style constraint/check for minimum redundancy with severity differentiated by task criticality.  
VERIFIED: TRUE

Definitive stance: the new material in this area is the admissible-count redundancy bug, heuristic ordering incompleteness, fail-open role defaults, zero-capacity inconsistency, and the disconnected probabilistic-feasibility path. The cross-component mutation concern is plausible but unverified from this scope.
